concerning-the-left-ventricle-select-the.explanation: The trabeculae carneae (muscular ridges lining the ventricular cavity) are coarser and more prominent in the right ventricle than in the left, not the other way round, so the statement that the left ventricle's are 'more than' the right ventricle's is false. Mechanistically, the right ventricle is a low-pressure volume pump whose wall relies more on trabecular architecture for contraction, while the thicker, high-pressure left ventricle has comparatively smoother inner walls apart from its papillary muscles. The takeaway is that thickness and trabeculation do not track together across the two ventricles: the left ventricle is the thicker chamber (about three times the right) but the right ventricle is the more heavily trabeculated one.

distractorNotes.A: Correctly true: the left ventricle wall is roughly three times thicker than the right, since it must generate systemic (not pulmonary) pressures.
distractorNotes.D: Correctly true: the left coronary artery's anterior interventricular (LAD) branch supplies the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum in most hearts.

conduction-speed-is-highest-in-the-bc0dd.explanation: Conduction velocity through the cardiac conduction system is fastest in the Purkinje fibres, reaching roughly 2-4 m/s, because their large diameter and abundant gap junctions let the depolarising wavefront spread almost instantly to the ventricular myocardium. This speed is functionally essential: it lets the Purkinje network deliver a near-simultaneous stimulus to both ventricles so they contract together rather than as a slow, disorganised wave. The takeaway ranking, from fastest to slowest, is Purkinje > atrial/internodal pathways > SA node > AV node, with the AV node deliberately the slowest link to allow ventricular filling before systole.

distractorNotes.A: The SA node conducts slowly relative to Purkinje tissue; its role is pacemaking, not rapid conduction.
distractorNotes.B: Internodal atrial bundles conduct faster than nodal tissue but far slower than Purkinje fibres.
distractorNotes.C: The AV node is the slowest-conducting tissue in the heart, the opposite of this question's answer.

conduction-speed-is-slowest-in-the-99b22.explanation: The AV node has the slowest conduction velocity in the heart, on the order of 0.05 m/s, because its small-diameter fibres and sparse gap junctions produce a deliberate conduction delay. This delay is physiologically purposeful: it gives the atria time to finish contracting and empty into the ventricles (the 'atrial kick') before the ventricles are electrically activated, optimising ventricular filling and stroke volume. The broader takeaway is that the conduction system trades speed for timing control at the AV node, in contrast to the Purkinje fibres, which are optimised purely for speed.

distractorNotes.A: The SA node conducts faster than the AV node; it is the pacemaker, not the delay point.
distractorNotes.B: Atrial pathways conduct impulses relatively quickly across the atria compared with the AV node.
distractorNotes.D: The Purkinje system is the fastest-conducting tissue in the heart, the opposite extreme from this question's answer.

during-the-heart-development-the-left-ho.explanation: During cardiac embryogenesis the sinus venosus has paired horns; as venous return is progressively redirected to the right side of the developing heart, the left horn regresses and its remnant becomes the coronary sinus (with its most proximal part forming the oblique vein of the left atrium, the vein of Marshall). This is the mirror-image event to the right horn, which instead enlarges and is incorporated into the right atrium as the smooth-walled sinus venarum. The takeaway is a left-right asymmetry rule worth memorising: right sinus horn becomes part of the right atrium; left sinus horn becomes the coronary sinus.

distractorNotes.B: The superior vena cava forms from the right common cardinal vein and right anterior cardinal vein, not the left sinus horn.
distractorNotes.C: The inferior vena cava's hepatic segment forms from the right vitelline vein, unrelated to the left sinus horn.
distractorNotes.D: The crista terminalis is a right atrial ridge marking the junction of the sinus venarum and the primitive atrium, a right-sided derivative, not a left-horn one.

one-of-the-following-does-not-open-into-.explanation: The azygos vein does not open directly into the right atrium; instead it arches over the root of the right lung and drains into the superior vena cava just before the SVC enters the atrium. The structures that do open directly into the right atrium are the superior vena cava, the inferior vena cava, the coronary sinus, and the small anterior cardiac veins (plus the minute thebesian veins). The takeaway is to distinguish tributaries that feed the great veins (like the azygos, which feeds the SVC) from vessels that have their own independent ostium in the atrial wall.

distractorNotes.B: Anterior cardiac veins drain the anterior right ventricle and open directly into the right atrium, usually through several small separate openings.
distractorNotes.C: The coronary sinus, draining most of the heart's venous blood, opens directly into the right atrium via its own ostium guarded by the thebesian valve.
distractorNotes.D: The superior vena cava opens directly into the upper part of the right atrium and has no valve guarding its orifice.

pacemaker-potentials-are-normally-absent.explanation: Pacemaker (spontaneous diastolic depolarisation) potentials are a property of the heart's specialised autorhythmic tissue -- the SA node, AV node, and Purkinje fibres -- which lack a stable resting potential and instead drift toward threshold via funny current and other ion channels. Working (contractile) myocardial cells, by contrast, have a stable resting membrane potential and depolarise only when an external wave of excitation reaches them; they do not generate spontaneous pacemaker activity under normal conditions. The clinical takeaway is that if working myocardium ever does develop pacemaker-like automaticity, it is abnormal (ectopic focus), which is why this property is specifically absent from normal working muscle.

distractorNotes.B: The SA node is the heart's dominant pacemaker and normally shows the fastest, most prominent pacemaker potentials.
distractorNotes.C: AV nodal cells possess pacemaker potentials too, acting as a backup (junctional) pacemaker if the SA node fails.
distractorNotes.D: Purkinje fibres retain latent pacemaker activity as a last-resort escape rhythm if higher pacemakers fail.

regarding-the-coronary-arteries-all-the-.explanation: In the great majority of hearts (right-dominant circulation, roughly 80-90% of people), the AV node is supplied by a branch of the RIGHT coronary artery, not the left, so the statement crediting the left coronary artery is the false one (the exception this EXCEPT-question is asking for). The other statements are standard coronary anatomy: the left coronary artery does arise from the left posterior aortic sinus, its anterior interventricular (LAD) branch does supply the interventricular septum's anterior part, and coronary perfusion is indeed greatest during ventricular diastole when extravascular compression is lowest. The exam takeaway is to keep AV-nodal supply (right-dominant in most people) separate from LAD/septal supply (left-dominant), since banks frequently test this exact swap.

distractorNotes.A: True: the left coronary artery arises from the left posterior aortic sinus, one of its defining anatomical facts.
distractorNotes.D: True: the anterior interventricular (LAD) artery is the left coronary artery's major branch supplying the anterior septum and anterior left ventricular wall.
distractorNotes.E: True: coronary blood flow, especially to the left ventricle, occurs predominantly during diastole because systolic compression of intramural vessels impedes flow.

systolic-pressure-in-right-ventricle-is-.explanation: Normal right ventricular systolic pressure is approximately 25 mmHg (typically cited in the 15-30 mmHg range), matching the pulmonary artery systolic pressure it generates against the low-resistance pulmonary circulation. This is roughly one-fifth of normal left ventricular systolic pressure (~120 mmHg), reflecting the pulmonary circuit's much lower vascular resistance compared with the systemic circuit. The physiological takeaway is that right and left ventricular systolic pressures should always be reasoned as a pair: the RV generates just enough pressure to perfuse the lungs, not the whole body.

distractorNotes.A: 35 mmHg is higher than the accepted normal RV systolic pressure and would suggest early pulmonary hypertension rather than a normal value.
distractorNotes.C: 15 mmHg is at the low end of normal RV diastolic filling pressure territory, not the systolic pressure the question asks about.

the-atrio-ventricular-valves-a-have-thre.explanation: The atrioventricular valves close when rising ventricular pressure during isovolumic contraction exceeds atrial pressure, forcing the cusps shut and preventing backflow into the atria; this is the correct physiological trigger described in option B. This is a passive, pressure-driven event, not something the papillary muscles cause: the papillary muscles and their chordae tendineae instead contract just before and during this closure to tether the cusps and stop them prolapsing back into the atria under high ventricular pressure. The exam takeaway is that valve opening and closing are governed by pressure gradients across the valve, while the papillary muscle-chordae apparatus only prevents prolapse -- it does not open or close the valve itself.

distractorNotes.C: False: papillary muscle contraction does not open the AV valves; the valves open passively when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure in diastole, and papillary contraction instead tensions the chordae during systole to prevent prolapse.

the-following-are-a-parts-of-the-conduct.explanation: The chordae tendineae are fibrous cords connecting the atrioventricular valve cusps to the papillary muscles; they are part of the mechanical valve-support apparatus, not the electrical conduction system, so they are the correct exception here. The true conduction system runs SA node to AV node to the bundle of His (atrioventricular bundle) to the Purkinje fibres, a specialised electrical pathway distinct from the heart's mechanical/structural components like valves and their supporting cords. The takeaway is to keep the heart's electrical scaffolding (nodes, bundle, Purkinje fibres) mentally separate from its mechanical scaffolding (valves, chordae, papillary muscles), since exam banks often test this exact distinction.

distractorNotes.A: Purkinje fibres are a genuine, terminal part of the conduction system, distributing the impulse into ventricular myocardium.
distractorNotes.B: The sinoatrial node is the heart's primary pacemaker and the conduction system's origin.
distractorNotes.D: The atrioventricular bundle (bundle of His) is a genuine conduction-system component linking the AV node to the bundle branches.
distractorNotes.E: The atrioventricular node is a genuine conduction-system component that delays and relays the impulse from atria to ventricles.

the-following-are-parts-of-the-conductiv.explanation: This is a duplicate of the identical question asking which listed structure is NOT part of the cardiac conduction system; the chordae tendineae remain the correct exception because they are mechanical valve-support cords, not electrical conduction tissue. The conduction pathway itself is SA node to AV node to bundle of His to Purkinje fibres, all of which are specialised myocardial cells adapted for impulse generation and rapid propagation rather than for anchoring a valve. As with the sibling question, the exam point is distinguishing electrical components of the heart from its purely mechanical, structural components.

distractorNotes.A: Purkinje fibres are the terminal, fastest-conducting part of the true conduction system.
distractorNotes.B: The sinoatrial node is the heart's dominant pacemaker and start of the conduction pathway.
distractorNotes.D: The atrioventricular bundle carries the impulse from the AV node into the ventricular conduction system.
distractorNotes.E: The atrioventricular node is the deliberate delay point between atrial and ventricular conduction.
